t.3.69.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Having heard the words of Sudeva, Ṛtuparṇa, lord of men, spoke to Bāhuka, soothing him with gentle speech.
t.3.69.2: I wish to go to the Vidarbhas, to Damayantī's self-choice ceremony, in a single day, O Bāhuka, you who know the true nature of horses, if you think it can be done.
t.3.69.3: O Kaunteya, when Nala had been addressed thus by that king, his heart was torn apart with grief, and the great-minded one sank into deep thought.
t.3.69.4: Could this be so? Damayantī, bewildered by grief, might do such a thing. Or else this may be a great stratagem devised for our sake.
t.3.69.5: Alas, the poor Vaidarbhī wishes to do a cruel thing, for she was wronged by me, petty, wicked and foolish as I am.
t.3.69.6: Fickle is the nature of women in this world, and my offence was grievous; it may be that she would act thus, helpless, her affection gone, the slender-waisted one shaken by grief for me and driven by despair.
t.3.69.7: She would never act thus, especially since she has children. Having gone there, I shall learn for certain what is true and fitting in this matter; I will fulfil Ṛtuparṇa's wish, and act for my own sake as well.
t.3.69.8: Having thus resolved in his mind, Bāhuka, downcast at heart, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words to Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of men.
t.3.69.9: I promise you truly, O lord of men: in a single day, O tiger among men, you shall reach the city of Vidarbha, O king.
t.3.69.10: Then, O king, Bāhuka went to the horse-stable at the command of King Bhāṅgasvari and made an examination of the horses.
t.3.69.11: Urged on repeatedly by Ṛtuparṇa to make haste, Bāhuka found horses that were lean yet strong, capable and enduring on the road.
t.3.69.12: Horses endowed with spirit and strength, possessed of good breeding and good temper, free of inferior marks, with wide nostrils and large jaws, pure in their ten curls of hair, born in Sindhu and swift as the wind.
t.3.69.14: How will these horses of mine, so feeble in strength and breath, draw me? And how is so great a distance to be travelled with steeds such as these?
t.3.69.13: Seeing them, the king, somewhat filled with anger, said: “What is this that you have sought to do? Are we, then, the ones to be deceived?”
t.3.69.15: Bāhuka said: These horses will reach the Vidarbhas; there is no doubt about this. But if you think otherwise, O king, tell me which others I should yoke for you.
t.3.69.16: You alone know the true nature of horses, and you are skilled, Bāhuka; quickly yoke those very ones that you consider capable.
t.3.69.17: Then the skilled man yoked to the chariot four excellent horses, endowed with good breeding and good temper and possessed of great speed.
t.3.69.18: Then the king, filled with haste, mounted the yoked chariot; and at once those excellent horses fell to the ground upon their knees.
t.3.69.19: Then, O lord of the people, the glorious King Nala, best of men, soothed those horses, which were endowed with energy and strength.
t.3.69.20: Taking up the reins and having the charioteer Vārṣṇeya mount the chariot, Nala, resorting to the utmost speed, set out eager to go.
t.3.69.22: But seeing those horses thus drawing the chariot with the swiftness of the wind, the wise lord of Ayodhyā was struck with the greatest amazement.
t.3.69.21: Urged on with skill by Bāhuka, those excellent horses flew up as if into the sky, as though bewildering the one who rode the chariot.
t.3.69.23: But hearing that rumble of the chariot and seeing that mastery in reining the horses, Vārṣṇeya pondered Bāhuka's knowledge of horses.
t.3.69.24: Could this perhaps be Mātali, the charioteer of the king of the gods? For such a great mark is seen in the hero Bāhuka.
t.3.69.25: Or might this be Śālihotra, who knows the true nature of the breeds of horses, having taken on a most splendid human form?
t.3.69.26: "Or could it perhaps be King Nala, conqueror of enemy cities? Has that very king come here?" Thus he pondered.
t.3.69.27: Or else, the very science that Nala knows, Bāhuka knows as well; for I perceive that the knowledge of Bāhuka and of Nala is equal.
t.3.69.29: For great-souled ones wander this earth in disguise, bound by a divine ordinance and by disfigurements prescribed in the scriptures.
t.3.69.28: Moreover, I think the age of this man and of Nala is the same. This is not the mighty Nala, yet he must be one who possesses that same knowledge.
t.3.69.31: His age and stature are the same, but in appearance he is the opposite; in the end I think Bāhuka is Nala, endowed with every virtue.
t.3.69.30: But my judgment would waver because of the deformity of his body; yet he may have become diminished from his proper stature, such indeed is my thought.
t.3.69.32: Having thus reflected in many ways, O great king, Vārṣṇeya, the charioteer of Puṇyaśloka, pondered deeply in his heart.
t.3.69.33: But King Ṛtuparṇa, O king of kings, reflecting on Bāhuka's knowledge of horses, rejoiced, together with his charioteer Vārṣṇeya.
t.3.69.34: Beholding that strength, valour and energy, that mastery of the horses, and that supreme effort, he attained the highest joy.
